paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and his spouse XXXX XXXX (First Associated Appellant), his adult son XXXX XXXX (Second Associated Appellant), [and three minor children XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associated Minor Appellants) appealed a May 18, 2018 decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) that rejected their claims for refugee protection from Ecuador and Afghanistan.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 BACKGROUND AND OVERVIEW OF APPEAL

The Principal Appellant, his spouse, and their adult son born in Afghanistan in 1997, fled Afghanistan in 2000 and were granted refugee status in Ecuador, where they became citizens in 2011. The minor Appellants were born in Ecuador in 2001, 2007 and 2009.
After arriving in Ecuador, the Principal Appellant opened and operated an Afghan restaurant with the help of UNHCR and in 2005 he developed a Bar Restaurant that expanded to a Discotheque.

The Appellants allege they have experienced a number of racially, religiously or ethnically motivated events of persecution in Ecuador, including the following incidents that were described in the Basis of Claim Form (BOC) and at the in-person RPD hearing. * In 2008, some people at the Discotheque refused to leave at closing time. After they were forced outside by security staff, the Principal Appellant went outside the Discotheque where he was injured by a bullet from one of the three individuals. He was hospitalized for treatment of a wound to his side and reported the incident to the police one week later.2 A perpetrator was never identified but after that incident the Principal Appellant denied entry to 'such people and or groups', thought to be Colombians or gang members, from entering his club. * In January 2012, the Principal Appellant was approached in his car by two armed people that he believed were Colombians. He accelerated his vehicle and escaped but not before one of them broke his car window with a pistol.3 The Appellant reported this incident to the police4 but no perpetrators were identified or charged. * Ongoing threats related to the Discotheque led the Appellant to stop the business and open a second hand clothes and furniture store. * In April 2014, the Appellant and his spouse were walking near their residence when two motorbike riders followed them and fired shots. A bullet hit his wife's hand. They sought medical treatment for her injury and reported the incident to police but no assailants were ever identified or prosecuted.5 * In January 2016, the Appellant was cleaning in front of his shop and a stranger insulted and threatened to kill him. The Appellant called the police who interviewed the stranger but took no further action. Later that day two Colombian men came to the shop and threatened him.6 * In August 2017, the Principal Appellant received a SMS/MMS death threat indicating the authors knew about him and his family.7 * The Principal Appellant's son, the associated Appellant, was injured in what appeared to be a racially motivated attack while at university.

The family left Ecuador, spent some time in Europe, and then traveled to the USA before coming to Canada. The family filed refugee claims upon entering Canada and the claims were referred to the RPD in September 2017 and decided on May 18, 2018. The appeal to the RAD was perfected on August 20, 2018.

There was a lengthy in-person hearing at the RPD in two sittings. The Appellants were represented by counsel and the Minister intervened. Accommodations were made to expedite the hearing and conduct the proceeding as informally as possible out of consideration for vulnerabilities of the Principle and First Associated Appellant related to each of them being diagnosed with PTSD. Medical reports were provided indicating accommodation needs. The RPD member heard evidence from the Principal Appellant, and the First and Second Associated Appellants, with appropriate interpreters arranged before the hearing and extensively amended at the hearing by adding a Spanish interpreter for the adult son and clarifying the needs related to Dari/Pashtu interpretation.

A claimant seeking refugee protection in Canada needs to establish that they have a well-founded fear of persecution because of a nexus ground [pursuant to section 96 of the IRPA] or that there is a specific risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment [pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA], in the country or countries of citizenship or former habitual residence. For Convention refugee status, claimants have to show that there is a serious possibility or reasonable chance of the alleged persecution if they return to their country. To establish that they are persons in need of protection, claimants have to show that there is a likelihood of the alleged risk on a balance of probabilities. If a section 96 persecution or section 97 risk is established, the claimants have to show that the state cannot provide adequate protection and that there is no reasonably safe alternative place to live in the country.

The Appellants claimed fear of persecution and harm in Ecuador and Afghanistan. Several elements for this claim are established without dispute, including identity, and citizenships in Ecuador and Afghanistan for the principal and adult associated Appellants and in Ecuador for the minor Appellants. The RPD member confirmed that the claim was focused on Ecuador and that if a claim was established for Ecuador, the claims were acceptable for the adult Appellants in relation to Afghanistan.

The hearing engaged evidence and submissions about Ecuador and canvassed issues including state protection and IFA, subjective fear and credibility, delay in departure, a well-founded fear of persecution, and the reasons for fearing and the likelihood of harm.

The RPD member found that there was a nexus to a Convention ground of race, nationality and religion because the Appellants are perceived as Arab and because they are Muslim. The RPD member examined whether the Appellants demonstrated a well-founded fear of persecution in Ecuador based on these Convention grounds concluded that the Appellants had faced discrimination but that it did not rise to the level of persecution and would not do so in future. The RPD member found that the Appellants were not prevented from accessing police, schools healthcare, travel, or practising their religion or operating successful businesses in Ecuador for a Convention ground. The member took note of the events of discrimination against the Appellants, including the physical attacks or threats they experienced, and found that the risk of harm did not rise to a level of persecution.

Regarding section 97, the RPD member concluded that the Appellants have a reasonable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Guayaquil, Ecuador's largest city that is far from Quito where the Appellants lived before leaving Ecuador. The RPD member identified that there were attacks against the Appellant related to his business because he turned away people perceived as gang members, with the assistance of his security personnel. The RPD member evaluated the specific incidents in light of that evidence and the fact of generalized, random violence in Ecuador and found it difficult to separate targeting related to the business practice from the generalized risks in Ecuador. In any event, the member found that the Appellants could reasonably live in Guayaquil, a city of close to three million people that is far from the place they lived before leaving Ecuador. The member found that the evidence did not establish they would be seriously harmed or sought after and, if there was specific targeting, the Appellants had not established that their attackers would seek them out in Guayaquil. It was not unreasonable for them to move to Guayaquil because the Principal Appellant could operate a business or work for someone else as he has successfully done in the past, the first associated Appellant is well-educated and has worked as a translator, and there are universities and schools for their children. Any risk of harm in Guayaquil is generalized and thus does not make moving there objectively unreasonable.
The RPD member did not make a finding regarding IFA for the purposes of section 96 because she found no serious possibility or reasonable chance of persecution for a Convention ground.

The Appellants did not submit new evidence to the RAD and did not request an oral hearing. They dispute the RPD member's subjective fear analysis under section 96, and take issue with specific factual findings and the conclusion of IFA in Guayaquil, although the Appellants' arguments do not specifically address the member's finding of that Guayaquil offers a reasonable IFA. Individual arguments are addressed in the analysis that follows.

As with most claims, a main source of evidence is the information from claimants, provided in a BOC and in oral evidence during the claim process, including at the RPD hearing. In this case, the Appellants described harassment, threats, insults and physical harm such as the attack on the second associate Appellant at his university, and the incidents involving the Principal Appellant and his spouse. They allege that the attacks against them are because of being perceived as Arabs, and for their religious beliefs, and that the attacks amount to persecution, or a risk of torture or harm. The Appellants did not argue that they are unable to practice their religion freely. They testified that there are two mosques in their locale, and their evidence is consistent with country documents confirming that freedom of religion is constitutionally guaranteed and generally respected in practice.8

In order to weigh evidence from the Appellants, it must be assessed for credibility. In this case, the RPD member concluded that the evidence provided by the three adult Appellants was credible and I agree with that assessment. Their information was consistent and logically presented, without apparent embellishment or confusion, and the Minister's representative who participated in the RPD hearing did not take a contrary view of their credibility.

The critical aspect for this appeal is about the probative value of the evidence. It is not enough for the Appellants to be credible in their account of events and experiences. They have a burden to show that their circumstances meet the essential elements for refugee protection. For the reasons given by the RPD member and taking into consideration the submissions for this appeal, I find the Appellants have failed to discharge that burden. I find that, while the Appellants have suffered discrimination in Ecuador because of their appearance, ethnicity or religion, the events and experiences do not show a serious possibility or likelihood of persecution or that they are persons in need of protection. I also agree with the RPD member that there is a reasonable IFA in Guayaquil for the reasons provided by the RPD member.
The following discussion addresses the Appellants' arguments in more detail. Argument a) The Member's subjective fear analysis under section 96 is contrary to law

The Appellants told the RPD member that the Principal Appellant's spouse and daughter wore hijab (scarf head coverings) when going to mosque on Fridays and that people made comments and called them Arab and other derogatory terms. In what she expressed to be a critical finding for her analysis of subjective fear, the RPD member found that, if the Appellants feared harm, they would not have let the Appellant's spouse and daughter wear the hijab in the streets but would have walked to the mosque without head covering and put it on before entering the mosque. The Appellants argue that the member's reasoning is unacceptable because requiring a claimant to suppress or hide a central part of her identity in order to avoid harm is anachronistic and contrary to law.

The RPD member's finding about the Appellant's spouse and daughter wearing the hijab was an evaluation of their past behaviour in the country of alleged persecution in order to assess subjective fear and the likelihood of future harm. It was not a suggestion that that they should suppress their identity or religious practice and beliefs or live discreetly and thus avoid persecution, which would be an error.

The cases cited by the Principal Appellant and examined by me for relevance to this appeal, confirm the principle that individuals should not be expected to hide sexual, religious or other essential features of identity. In Fosu,9 the issue was IFA and the court rejected the member's expectation that the Appellant could live discreetly as a homosexual in a country where homosexuality is against the law. That case was cited in Sadeghi-Pari,10 in response to the board's suggestion that the lesbian claimant could live safely in Iran if she maintained secrecy. That was a relatively inconsequential error in the judicial review, which was allowed for many implausibility and non-credibility findings underlying the member's conclusion that the claimant was not really a lesbian. The case of V.S.11 was a PRRA decision for a lesbian woman pending removal to Cameroon, where homosexuality is against the law. The judicial review was granted because the officer erred in assuming that the claimant could avoid difficulty in Cameroon by concealing her sexual identity. The same point was made in Jasim,12 where the main problem was a lack of reasons given in the H&C application but the FC also pointed out the error of suggesting that the claimant could live safely in Bahrain if he refrained from proselytizing and practiced his faith privately. Similarly, in Mohebbi,13 the court confirmed that it was not for the RPD to determine how the claimant should practice his belief in response to the RPD's conclusion that the claimant would have to be discreet about his Christianity in Iran.

The cases were not assessing past behaviour to evaluate subjective fear and they do not stand for the principle that a board member may not consider past behaviour of a claimant to assess subjective fear.

The case of Gur14 is the most similar to this appeal: the Federal Court impugned the RPD's analysis of whether discriminatory treatment of the Alevi and Kurdish claimant in Turkey amounted to persecution. The decision was quashed because the member misapprehended the testimony and evidence of the claimant. Also somewhat instructive is the case of Mu15 regarding a PRRA application for a Falun Gong practitioner under removal to China. The case reiterates the principal that fundamental beliefs should not need to be hidden, and the court found the main error was that the officer used the wrong standard of proof and assessed the claimant's words rather than his actions.

Freedom of religion requires that people be able to openly practice their faith without fear of reprisals. All of the cited cases affirm the principle that these Appellants cannot be expected to renounce their deeply held beliefs or refrain from exercising their fundamental rights in order to avoid persecution and thus live securely in Ecuador. However, the cases do not stand for the principle that past behaviour cannot be evaluated in order to assess subjective fear. I find no error in the RPD member's assessment of that: she took note that the Appellants did not wear a hijab routinely but did so on their way to the mosque on Friday and considered that evidence in relation to their alleged fear. Other evidence assessed by the RPD member in relation to subjective fear included that the Principal Appellant's successful restaurant and Discotheque businesses were called XXXX XXXX Restaurant and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX [XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX], which advertised and promoted his foreign nationality and ethnicity.16

The Appellants have not shown that the RPD member erred in her assessment about subjective fear. The experiences they described about their life in Ecuador is reliable evidence that is relevant to evaluating a likelihood of forward-looking persecution. It is not unreasonable to consider the public wearing of a hijab or promoting their ethnicity or nationality in the businesses as behavioural indicators about whether the Appellants lived in personal fear during their day to day activities. Argument b) The Member downplayed the significance of the vicious attack on XXXX XXXX (the Appellant's son)

The Second Associated Appellant testified that he has been threatened and insulted many times on account of being perceived as Arab, at university or on the streets. He described two occasions when he called police: once when he saw a person break his car window and another when thieves broke into the office at his father's restaurant trying to steal computers. He also described that he and other middle-east restaurant workers were insulted by patrons of restaurant where he worked, and by people who would see his sister and mother wearing head-covering. He described random people insulting the family with words and threatening signs. On one occasion, he was physically attacked at the bus station near his university in the late evening, about two hours away from the family home. This event in March 2016 involved five young strangers on motorcycles who called him an Arab and beat him with their motorcycle helmets. This Appellant said he did not report the incident to police because he did not trust the police to help, and he testified that he believes he will encounter similar harassment in the future based on his features, accent and name.

The RPD member found that the beating at the bus stop was by gang members for racist reasons and concluded that it was a random act of violence in a country where "there is a lot of random violence and gangs attack people generally for no reasons in Ecuador".17 Based on the description of the incident, this is an accurate characterization that was not materially disputed by the Appellants. The Second Associated Appellant did not know his attackers and did not see them before or since the attack.

The Appellants submit that it was a contradiction for the RPD member to find that the motorcycle attack on the Second Associated Appellant was a random act of violence and then to state that it was for racist reasons. They suggest that the conclusion of a random act of violence is inconsistent with finding it was racially motivated and that people such as the Appellants, who are perceived as refugees, suffer high levels of discrimination. They argue that the RPD member erroneously downplayed this attack and the negative and derogatory statements made by the perpetrators because she was unable to find evidence in the country documents of physical attacks against Muslims and those perceived as Arabs and refugees. The Appellants point out that there is not a sizeable population of Afghani Muslims like the Appellants who are perceived as being Arabs because almost all the refugees in Ecuador originate from Colombia. A Human Rights Report found that refugees in Ecuador, especially women and children, experienced sexual and gender-based violence and reported the forced recruitment of adolescents into criminal activity, such as drug trafficking and robbery, on the northern border, particularly by organized criminal gangs that also operated in Colombia.18 Some of the random events described by the Appellants are consistent with the type of gang activity referred to in the documents, but their circumstances are otherwise not similar to those that affect other migrants or refugees described in this document.

The Principal Appellant confirmed that, in Ecuador, the term 'Arab' is used against foreigners without distinction, and includes people from Central Asia, Pakistan and India. He and his family also confirmed that there is random violence or harassment against all perceived foreigners in Ecuador. He offered the possibility that the events in 2014, when a man broke a bottle outside his clothing store and threatened to kill him because he was an Arab and when two men later came into his clothing store with threats to harm him, may have been related to the Disco business.19 There were no further events until more than 1.5 years later, when the text message was sent to the Principal Appellant. The Appellants did not connect that text message to other incidents or to any specific reason for targeting: the Principal Appellant was asked but could offer no insight as to why he received that text or the reason for any of the other incidents of harm or threats of harm against himself and his family.

The Appellant's argue that the member erred in relying on scarce country condition documentation to support her conclusions but I disagree. It does not logically follow that a lack of information about the specific personal attributes of the Appellants should mean that they experience higher levels of discrimination than the groups who are specifically identified in country condition documents as vulnerable groups in Ecuador. Furthermore and in any event, random or general violence that has a racial undertone is not an inconsistent concept and can be reasonably distinguished from targeted persecution toward the Appellants for a nexus ground. An act of violence accompanied by racist slurs offers some suggestion about the perpetrator's thoughts or motivation but that part of the conduct is not sufficient to make an inference of persecutory harm toward the Appellants for a nexus ground. Other than connection with the Principal Appellant's business practice of denying entry of gang or gang-appearing persons into his Discotheque, the incidents described by the Appellants are more consistent with random violence or discrimination than with specifically targeted harm toward them. I have searched for information and not found specific reference in the country documents to the specific category of Muslims from Afghanistan who are perceived as Arabs, nor have the Appellants pointed out such reference. Thus, it may be true that the profile of the Appellants is not specifically canvassed in the country condition information. However, that fact does not demand an inference that their victimization is persecution rather than the generalized random violence or discrimination facing other residents of Ecuador.

The difference between persecution, which may form the basis for refugee protection, and discrimination or harassment, which does not, is the degree of seriousness of the harm. To make the distinction, I considered the perpetrator's actions and their effect because, typically, it cannot be known what was in the minds of the perpetrators. Events may amount to persecution if cruelty was inflicted repeatedly and persistently or in a systematic way, for a nexus ground. Repetition is not necessary, however, as in some cases the serious quality of specific incidents will constitute a fundamental violation of human dignity.

My own examination of events the Appellants have credibly described is that they have suffered a type of discrimination and random violence generally present in Ecuador. I find that the evidence was weighed correctly by the RPD member, who considered seriousness and looked for systematic indicators in an effort to distinguish what the Appellants experienced from the generalized risks affecting all residents of Ecuador. During the RPD hearing, the member enquired extensively of each of the adult Appellants if they had a sense or idea who might have targeted them and no specifics were forthcoming: each Appellant suggested general or random violence, accidental harm or, to a limited extent, that some events may have been a response to the business practice of denying entry to those perceived as gang members. The Appellants themselves have attributed their experiences to the random or accidental violence that exists in Ecuador from gangs or Colombians. They also suggested possible repercussions for the business practice of denying entry to gang members at the Discotheque. In totality, the evidence about specific events and incidents is more consistent with random violence than with specific targeting other than in relation to the business practice of the Principal Appellant, which was also generalized and non-specific discrimination.

The Appellants argued that they cannot rely on the police and do not have confidence the police can protect them but that is not supported by the evidence. The Second Associated Appellant said he chose not to call the police after being physically harmed because they are ineffective and the Principal Appellant also alleged police ineffectiveness because they did not find the perpetrators. The perception of the Appellants that they do not have police support is subjective and not supported by the evidence. They have inferred police ineffectiveness from the fact that police did not identify and apprehend perpetrators but that is not sound logic. The inability of police to apprehend or identify perpetrators does not equate to persecution or harm or raise the seriousness of the reported incidents to a level of persecution. The Second Associated Appellant's evidence was that on the two occasions when he reported vandalism incidents to police, they responded, took information, and looked for the thieves. He confirmed that the police responded to his calls as they would respond for anyone in Ecuador and that they treated him respectfully. The Principal Appellant had a similarly positive experience when the police attended at his place of business after his report of vandalism and threats.

The Appellants did not establish that the beating incident against the Second Associated Appellant was personal targeting or that he would be persecuted in the future. They confirmed that he did not have trouble with teachers or public services, admission to university, treatment from professors, or access to public services because of a perceived nationality as Arab or for his ethnicity or religion. He confirmed that on two previous occasions when he called the police they responded, took information and searched for the perpetrators. They treated him with respect. They did not treat him differently from how other people in Ecuador are treated by police. The evidence about his experience does not disclose systematic or institutional discrimination for a Convention ground or that he is personally at risk of harm or torture in Ecuador. The Principal Appellant's experience also confirmed the effectiveness of local police. The Appellants testified that the police responded to reported incidents of harm and vandalism respectfully and with follow-up investigations and they have enjoyed economic stability and success, access to all services, schools, and other personal and economic freedoms including the ability to attend mosque.

The burden was on the Appellants to show that the violence or discrimination toward them amounts to persecution. That burden is not discharged by simply pointing out that their unique profile is not specifically identified in the country documents. They acknowledged that a random and generalized type of violence exists in Ecuador but have not identified specific, systematic or sustained acts of discrimination or harm because of their unique profile such that they are set apart from and not simply subject to the general risk of violence that affects everyone living in Ecuador. Argument c) The Member's finding that the multiple physical attacks and threats against the parents were not racially motivated is untenable

The RPD member found that the reason for the shootings and death threats "has something to do with" the Appellant's business and refusing to serve gang members at the discotheque for some years.20 The Appellants acknowledge this but allege racism played a part as well. More importantly, the Appellants point out that after the Appellant closed his club in 2013, he opened up a second-hand clothing and furniture store. The Appellants argue that it was an error for the Member to attribute the 2013 to 2017 threats and violent incidents to his denying entry to gang members at the Discotheque because of events that happened after the Discotheque was closed: there was a shooting in 2014 when his wife was hurt and a death threat in 2016.

The argument is incorrect based on my review of the hearing audio. The Principal Appellant testified that he did not know who shot at him and hit his wife in the 2014 incident, or who was responsible for the 2017 incidents, but himself suggested that it might have related to the Discotheque business and Colombian gangs.21 Furthermore and in any event, even if the events after 2013 were randomly motivated incidents not connected to the operation of the Discotheque, there is less rather than more probative evidence that the events are persecutory rather than random generalized risk affecting all residents of Ecuador.

The Appellant's argument does not disclose any error in the RPD member's decision. The member acknowledged that racism played a part in the events but found that this was discrimination, not persecution, which leads to the next argument. Argument d) The Member's discrimination v. persecution analysis is flawed

The Appellants allege that the RPD member improperly dismissed the physical violence and attacks against the parents and against their adult son as not being racially motivated. They argue that by doing so, the member was able to find that the racist comments and anti-Muslim words against the Appellants did not rise to the level of persecution. The Appellants argue that, when the physical attacks and death threats are taken together with the daily racist and anti-Muslim comments, there is no doubt that the Appellants experienced persecution and are at risk of being persecuted in the future on Convention grounds.

I disagree with the Appellants' position and find that the RPD member did not err in her analysis of persecution vs. discrimination. Persecution is sustained or systemic violation of basic human rights in a fundamental way. The member took note that the Appellants have not been denied access to education, healthcare, or the ability to rent or purchase accommodation in Ecuador, since arriving there in 2000. The Principal Appellant has not been prevented from operating his businesses and the family has enjoyed financial and economic success. They are not prevented from practising their religion. The children participate socially and are not ostracized as Muslims, Arabs or Afghan children.

The Appellants have suffered discrimination but not persecution. Looking forward, the evidence does not show reasonable chance or serious possibility of persecution. The RPD member took note, and I agree, that there is a general risk of violence in Ecuador and that the risk faced by the Appellants is not different from what others face in Ecuador. The Appellants have not shown how the RPD member's analysis was incorrect or that the evidence leads to conclusion of persecution rather than discrimination. Argument e) the member's finding that the Appellants did not take steps to protection themselves is unfounded

The Appellants argue that the member was wrong to say that the Appellants "don't take steps to protect themselves because they're afraid, as Muslims, or perceived to [be] Arabs or refugees".22 They point out that the Appellant closed his business, that they contacted the police on many occasions to protect themselves, that the Appellant armed himself with a pistol, and that the family eventually left Ecuador.

The Appellants have taken the RPD member's statement out of context. The member was evaluating whether their fundamental human right to practise their religion was interfered with and found that they did not face systemic discrimination in that regard. The Member pointed out that the Appellants were not prevented them from openly practising their religion or advertising their business, that the children were not ostracized because of being Muslim or Afghan or perceived as Arab, and pointed out that the family did not take steps to protect themselves out of fear because of those attributes. This is not to say that the Appellants did not experience incidents of discrimination or random attacks such as occur generally in Ecuador. As previously discussed, the distinction between persecution and discrimination includes a need to evaluate and characterize evidence about past events and experiences taking into consideration the country conditions, which the RPD member did correctly in this case.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
